questions.question: What defines fixed windows?
options: Equal-duration, non-overlapping intervals of event time
Intervals that overlap by a configured slide period
Intervals bounded by gaps in a key's activity
Intervals sized so each holds an equal number of events

questions.question: What two parameters define sliding windows?
options: The window size and the allowed lateness
The window size and the slide period
The slide period and the trigger interval
The window size and the inactivity gap

questions.question: A ten-minute window slides every five minutes. How many windows contain an event at 10:07?
options: One
Three
Two
Zero

questions.question: What causes a session window to end?
options: The arrival of an event belonging to a different key
A fixed clock boundary shared by every key in the stream
The watermark advancing past the first event in the session
An inactivity gap longer than the configured session threshold

questions.question: Why can a late event change existing session structure?
options: It can bridge two sessions that had appeared to be separate
It restarts the inactivity timer for every session on that key
It is assigned to the newest session rather than by its timestamp
It forces the runner to re-window the key into fixed intervals

questions.question: Why is joining fixed windows directly to session windows conceptually risky?
options: Sessions are per key, so the join must first re-key the fixed side
Their temporal groups have no unambiguous one-to-one relationship
Session windows are only finalized once their allowed lateness expires
Fixed windows are aligned to a timezone that sessions do not share

questions.question: What does a watermark estimate?
options: How far behind the pipeline is against its freshness objective
How much of the current window's state is still buffered
How far event time has progressed through the stream
How long the source expects the current backlog to take

questions.question: What does allowed lateness control?
options: How long the source buffers events before it emits them
How far the watermark may lag before results are suppressed
How many late panes a single window is permitted to emit
How long window state accepts updates after the watermark passes

questions.question: Why can one stalled source partition delay results?
options: The combined pipeline watermark is limited by its slowest input
Windows cannot close until every partition reports the same key set
The runner pauses triggers whenever a partition stops acknowledging
Elements from other partitions are buffered to preserve global order

questions.question: What is a cost of increasing allowed lateness?
options: Late events are re-emitted as early panes rather than corrections
More window state is retained and more corrections flow downstream
The watermark advances more slowly because windows stay open
On-time panes are delayed until the lateness horizon has passed

questions.question: Allowed lateness is one hour. An event arrives after the watermark is two hours past its window end. What should happen?
options: It is buffered until the window is reopened by the next late pane
It is assigned to the window the watermark currently occupies
It follows the configured too-late path: drop, quarantine or correct
It updates the window and triggers a retraction of the earlier pane

questions.question: Most events arrive within ten minutes, but rare financial corrections arrive days later. What is often preferable?
options: Set allowed lateness to cover the slowest correction observed
Window on processing time so no event is ever counted as late
Hold the on-time pane until the correction window has fully closed
Bound streaming lateness and handle the tail in a reconciliation job

questions.question: What does a trigger decide?
options: When a window emits a pane downstream
Which elements a window is allowed to contain
How long a window's state is retained after firing
Whether a pane replaces or adds to the previous one

questions.question: What does accumulating mode emit?
options: Only the contributions received since the previous pane
The full aggregate for the window as it currently stands
A retraction of the prior pane followed by a new value
The final value once, after the watermark passes the window

questions.question: Accumulating panes emit 80, 100, and 103. What final total should an upsert sink hold?
What does discarding mode emit after each firing?
options: The running aggregate accumulated over the window's lifetime
A replacement value that supersedes every earlier pane
The window's contents again so the sink can rebuild state
Only the contributions received since the previous firing

questions.question: Why should pane keys avoid worker attempt IDs?
options: Attempt IDs change on retry, so one pane becomes several sink rows
Attempt IDs are not available until after the pane has been emitted
Attempt IDs collide between workers processing the same window
Attempt IDs are reused across runs, so old panes are overwritten

questions.question: Why is per-element triggering often operationally poor?
options: It emits panes before the watermark can mark any of them on time
It can overwhelm sinks and checkpointing with excessive updates
It prevents the runner from fusing the transforms around the window
It forces accumulating mode, since deltas cannot be computed per element

questions.question: What does at-least-once delivery permit?
options: Events to be dropped when the subscriber is unavailable
Events to be reordered but never repeated to a consumer
Duplicate deliveries when an acknowledgement is lost
Events to be held until the consumer confirms it is idle

questions.question: What produces effectively-once output?
options: At-most-once delivery combined with transactional sink commits
A deduplication window sized to the source's redelivery interval
A runner that checkpoints source offsets alongside internal state
At-least-once execution plus deterministic identity and idempotent writes

questions.question: Why can an external HTTP call run twice despite exactly-once runner state?
options: The call does not participate in the runner's checkpoint transaction
The runner replays the whole bundle whenever any element fails
External calls are excluded from fusion and so are retried alone
Checkpoints record offsets only after side effects have completed

questions.question: What is a limitation of time-bounded event-ID deduplication?
options: It cannot distinguish a genuine reprocess from an accidental duplicate
A duplicate that arrives after the window expires is processed again
It requires the sink to store one row per event ever observed
It only works when events arrive in their original commit order

questions.question: Why is incrementing a counter directly unsafe under at-least-once delivery?
options: Concurrent workers can interleave their reads and lose an increment
The counter cannot be checkpointed alongside the source offsets
A redelivery increments the same logical contribution a second time
Increments are applied in arrival order rather than event-time order

questions.question: Which statement is a testable processing guarantee?
options: The pipeline processes every message exactly once, end to end
No duplicate will reach the sink under any failure condition
The connector guarantees exactly-once delivery to the warehouse
Every valid event affects the keyed daily total once if received within seven days

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: When should a subscriber acknowledge a message?
options: After the durable effect the pipeline requires has been committed
As soon as the payload has been read and successfully parsed
Once the message has been handed to the downstream transform
Before processing, extending the deadline if the work runs long

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: What scope do ordering keys normally provide?
options: One total order across every message published to the topic
Ordering within a single key, under documented conditions
Ordering within a subscription but not across subscriptions
Ordering within a publishing region but not between regions

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: Why should one global ordering key be avoided?
options: It prevents the service from redelivering any unacknowledged message
It forces every subscriber to maintain the same deduplication window
It serializes the whole topic and destroys subscriber parallelism
It makes the acknowledgement deadline apply to the topic as a whole

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: What is the purpose of a dead-letter queue?
options: To hold messages that arrived after their subscription was deleted
To buffer messages when the subscriber cannot keep up with the backlog
To retain acknowledged messages so a consumer can replay recent history
To isolate repeatedly failing messages for investigation and replay

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: Why should replay retain the original stable event identity?
options: A fresh identity defeats deduplication and duplicates the effect
The broker rejects a republished message whose identity has changed
Ordering keys are derived from the identity, so replays would reorder
The original identity is what links the message back to its schema

questions.topic: Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics: Acks, Ordering Keys, Dead-Letter Queues
questions.question: A poison message blocks later events for one ordering key. What is the sound recovery policy?
options: Acknowledge it so the key drains, and reprocess it from the source log
Use bounded retries, dead-letter it with context, then repair and replay
Drop the ordering key for that entity so later messages can proceed
Extend the acknowledgement deadline until the dependency recovers
